title: At the market — prices and bargaining
title_target: দাম কত? একটু কমান — dam kôt? èk-Tu kô-man
goal: Ask prices, bargain without giving offense, and say weights and quantities — in sentences short enough that you'll really use them.
bekal: ask prices with দাম কত and কেজি কত
bargain with একটু কমান and শেষ দাম কত
praise and complain about goods: টাটকা, পচা, বেশি দাম
know where bargaining is fine and where it isn't

dialogs.title: কথোপকথন — Bargaining for mangoes
dialogs.intro: Mango season has arrived and Ani tries bargaining for the first time. Listen to the tone: bargaining in Bengal is a friendly exchange, not a fight.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Brother, how much are the mangoes?

lines.speaker: বিক্রেতা:
lines.id: A hundred and twenty a kilo. Really fresh, from Rajshahi.
lines.literal: kilo — hundred — twenty. totally — fresh, Rajshahi's.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: A hundred and twenty? Isn't that a bit much?

lines.speaker: বিক্রেতা:
lines.id: Sister, everyone at the market is charging a hundred and thirty.
lines.literal: sister, market-at — everyone — hundred — thirty — is-taking.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Come down a little! I'll take two kilos.
lines.literal: a-little — lower-please — na! two — kilo — will-take.

lines.speaker: বিক্রেতা:
lines.id: If you take two kilos, a hundred and ten. That's my last price.
lines.literal: two — kilo — if-take — hundred — ten. this-very — last — price.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Make it a hundred. I'll come every day.

lines.speaker: বিক্রেতা:
lines.id: Ha ha! All right, for you a hundred and five.
lines.literal: ha ha! okay, your — for — hundred — five.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Fine. And give me one hali of eggs.
lines.literal: right — is. and — one — hali — egg — give-please.

lines.speaker: বিক্রেতা:
lines.id: Fifty a hali. That's two hundred and sixty altogether.
lines.literal: hali — fifty. all — together — two-hundred — sixty.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Here's three hundred. Do you have change?

lines.speaker: বিক্রেতা:
lines.id: Yes, forty back. Come again, sister!
lines.literal: is-there, forty — back. again — will-come(polite) — sister!

notes: **Bargaining in Bengal is a conversation, not a battle.** The tone is light, often broken by laughter, and it almost always ends with both sides feeling they won a little. ⚠️ Bargaining with a hard face or naming a price far too low actually ends the conversation — not because the money offends anyone, but because it spoils the tone of the meeting.

⚠️ **Some places are not for bargaining.** At a **বাজার** (open market), fruit carts, cloth shops and rickshaws, bargaining is normal and expected. At a **দোকান** with price tags, supermarkets, pharmacies and restaurants, the price is fixed and bargaining feels awkward. A simple rule: **if the number is printed, don't bargain.**

**The most effective bargaining line isn't a number but a relationship.** “আমি রোজ আসব” (I'll come every day) and “আমি এখানেই থাকি” (I live right here) work far better than naming a low price. Bengali traders deal in regular customers, not one-off sales.

**একটু কমান না!** *èk-Tu kô-man na* is the bargaining line you'll hear most. ⚠️ Note the **না** at the end: here it is **not** a negative but a softener, like “come on” in “come down a little, come on”. The pitch falls, not rises. Say না with a rising pitch and it means “no” again.

**There are four units of weight you need.** **কেজি** (kilogram) is used everywhere. **পোয়া** *poa* is a quarter kilo — 250 grams — and is very common for chilies, ginger and spices. **হালি** *hali* means **four pieces**, and is almost always used for eggs and limes. ⚠️ Don't be surprised to hear “one hali” — it isn't a weight but a count of four.

**ভাংতি** *bhangti* means small change, and it's a real everyday problem.** Small traders often have no change for big notes, and the sentence **ভাংতি নেই** (no change) can stop a sale. ⚠️ Keep small notes; asking **ভাংতি আছে?** before handing over a big one is a habit that makes you look like a local.

**টাটকা** *TaTka* — fresh — is the compliment traders value most, and its opposite **পচা** *pôcha* (rotten) is the complaint they fear most. If the goods aren't great, don't say পচা; just say **এটা ভালো না** (this isn't good) or point to another with **ওটা দিন** (give me that one).

grammars.title: Asking prices and bargaining

head: বাংলা
Say it
Meaning
rows: All right, give it to me.
Never mind, I don't need it.

after: ⚠️ **থাক, লাগবে না is the gentlest way to back out.** Literally “let it be, it's not needed”. Say it with a smile and step away slowly; the seller will often call you back with a better price. If not, you still part on good terms.

grammars.title: Weights, quantities and money
after: **To say “how much each”, use কত করে** *kôt kô-ré* — literally “how much by doing”. এটা কত করে? is a sentence you'll use again and again, and the answer usually takes the form “… টাকা করে”.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Four things to know at a Bengali market
items: **আম isn't just a fruit in Bengal — it's a season.** Between May and July people discuss mango varieties the way others discuss football: হিমসাগর, ল্যাংড়া, ফজলি, আম্রপালি. Asking **কোন আম সবচেয়ে ভালো?** opens a long, happy conversation.

**কাঁঠাল is the national fruit of Bangladesh** — the jackfruit, a huge green fruit with sweet yellow pods. Mention that it grows in your country too (or that you've tried it) and you'll make a friend on the spot.
**গামছা is a thin checked cotton cloth used for everything** — towel, headband, seat mat, strainer. It's cheap, light, and a far more memorable souvenir than a key ring.
⚠️ **Don't handle and squeeze the fruit.** Just point with **ওটা দেখান** (show me that one) and let the seller pick it up. Choosing for yourself while squeezing is seen as a bit rude at many stalls.

blocks.text: A note on money in Bangladesh. The currency is the **টাকা**, and notes run from ২ to ১০০০. The numbers on the notes are written in **Bengali numerals**, not Western ones — so the script pages at the front of this book will be put to work right away in your wallet. For small payments cash is still king; but **বিকাশ** *bikash*, the mobile wallet almost everyone uses, has replaced coins at many stalls.

exercises.prompt: Choose the right answer for each situation: bargain (হ্যাঁ) or don't bargain (না).
items: At a pharmacy with printed prices → ____

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

items: Never mind, I don't need it.

answers: আমের দাম কত? — আমি দুই কেজি নেব। — এটাই শেষ দাম। — আপনার কি ভাংতি আছে? — আমি রোজ আসব।
কেজি কত? — একটু কমান না। — আমি দুই কেজি নেব। — সব মিলে কত? — ভাংতি আছে? — থাক, লাগবে না।
